\boxed_review{
## Summary:

This paper delves into the critical issue of out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, specifically examining the brittleness of robustness under varying degrees of distribution shifts. The authors challenge the common assumption that better performance on moderate distribution shifts implies better performance on more extreme shifts. Through a series of experiments on image classification tasks using datasets like NoisyMNIST, RotatedMNIST, NoisyImageNet15, and LR-ImageNet15, they demonstrate that models exhibiting strong performance on datasets with mild shifts can exhibit surprisingly poor performance on datasets with more severe shifts. This observation highlights a significant vulnerability in current OOD generalization methods, suggesting that models may not be as robust as previously assumed when faced with more diverse or challenging data. Furthermore, the study investigates the behavior of pre-trained models, such as CLIP, under novel distribution shifts and finds them to be particularly sensitive, often performing worse than randomly initialized models on datasets with unseen shifts. The core methodology involves training various models, including CNNs, ResNets, and ViTs, on datasets with controlled degrees of distribution shift and then evaluating their performance on test sets with different shift magnitudes. The main empirical findings reveal a consistent pattern of performance degradation as the degree of distribution shift increases, even for models that perform well under less extreme conditions. This brittleness is not merely a matter of model architecture or training strategy, but rather a fundamental property of OOD generalization. The authors also explore the impact of different training strategies, such as linear probing, on the observed robustness. The overall significance of this work lies in its identification of a critical flaw in current OOD generalization practices, emphasizing the need for more robust evaluation protocols and methods that can handle the complexities of real-world distribution shifts. The paper's findings underscore the importance of considering the full spectrum of possible distribution shifts, rather than focusing on limited ranges, and highlight the limitations of current pre-trained models in handling truly novel scenarios. meta_review.summary: This paper delves into the critical issue of out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, specifically examining the brittleness of robustness under varying degrees of distribution shifts. The authors challenge the common assumption that better performance on moderate distribution shifts implies better performance on more extreme shifts. Through a series of experiments on image classification tasks using datasets like NoisyMNIST, RotatedMNIST, NoisyImageNet15, and LR-ImageNet15, they demonstrate that models exhibiting strong performance on datasets with mild shifts can exhibit surprisingly poor performance on datasets with more severe shifts. This observation highlights a significant vulnerability in current OOD generalization methods, suggesting that models may not be as robust as previously assumed when faced with more diverse or challenging data. Furthermore, the study investigates the behavior of pre-trained models, such as CLIP, under novel distribution shifts and finds them to be particularly sensitive, often performing worse than randomly initialized models on datasets with unseen shifts. The core methodology involves training various models, including CNNs, ResNets, and ViTs, on datasets with controlled degrees of distribution shift and then evaluating their performance on test sets with different shift magnitudes. The main empirical findings reveal a consistent pattern of performance degradation as the degree of distribution shift increases, even for models that perform well under less extreme conditions. This brittleness is not merely a matter of model architecture or training strategy, but rather a fundamental property of OOD generalization. The authors also explore the impact of different training strategies, such as linear probing, on the observed robustness. The overall significance of this work lies in its identification of a critical flaw in current OOD generalization practices, emphasizing the need for more robust evaluation protocols and methods that can handle the complexities of real-world distribution shifts. The paper's findings underscore the importance of considering the full spectrum of possible distribution shifts, rather than focusing on limited ranges, and highlight the limitations of current pre-trained models in handling truly novel scenarios. This work serves as a valuable contribution to the field by exposing the fragility of current OOD methods and pointing towards the need for more robust approaches.
